title: January-February warmth had no clear common link to the gap between butterfly and swallow sightings at 69 Japan stations in 1953-2020
abstract: We tested whether January-February warmth changed the gap between first butterfly and first barn swallow sightings in Japan. We used 4,077 paired station-years at 69 fixed stations in 1953-2020. Four separate North and South, early and late models removed station-by-location-code and year effects. Slopes ranged from -5.78 to +0.51 days per C. All four adjusted uncertainty intervals included zero. The early southern marginal interval was negative, but the planned repeated-association rule failed. Station trends, adjacent-year differences, and January-only checks did not give a common link. Hypothetical independent report delays of 0.17-1.28 days permit zero slopes in the fixed-record models. These are possibility bounds, not estimates of real delay. Missing pairs, abundance and detection, coarse weather, current coordinates, and small residual weather contrasts limit inference. We do not estimate feeding overlap, air pollution, daily extremes, or causal climate-change effects. The package includes source event tables, an audited panel, weather extracts, source hashes, code, all estimates, figures, and independent numerical checks.

display.caption: Four separate estimates for butterfly day minus swallow day per 1 C of January-February warmth. All four adjusted intervals include zero. Intervals use the largest station, year, or two-way cluster variance and a four-test correction. Their coverage is approximate.

Annual recorded gaps after station means are removed. Red curves are seven-year means. Unequal records and detection can affect these descriptive patterns. The curves do not estimate a climate effect.
